studies.title: Second Of Two In The Cave
studies.meaning: The sentence opens with a conditional that is almost a shrug: if you do not help him, he has been helped already. What follows is a memory offered as evidence, told in a chain of clauses each beginning with when, which holds the scene in the present. The reassurance quoted is a single short sentence. Then four things God is said to have done, none of them visible at the time to the two men inside the rock.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage urging a community reluctant to set out on a hard expedition. The memory recalled is the migration from Mecca, when the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and one companion hid in a cave while search parties looked for them. The commentators treat the reference as well known to its audience, which is why no narrative detail is given beyond what the argument needs.

keyTerms.note: A hollow in rock rather than a cavern, the kind of shelter a traveller uses. The definite article assumes the hearer knows which one, so the ayah is recalling a story rather than telling it.
From a root for settling and stillness, related to the word for a dwelling. It names a calm that descends and settles rather than one a person achieves, which is why the verb used is sending down.
A superlative in the feminine, matching the word for an utterance. Two claims are set on a vertical scale, and the outcome is described as a position occupied rather than as an argument won.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pursuit in the desert was a tracking skill. Bedouin trackers could read a person's weight, pace and direction from disturbed sand, and Mecca offered a substantial bounty for the two men. Hiding in country you did not control meant sitting still while people who knew the ground searched it. The cave lay south of the city, against the expected direction of flight.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for tranquillity appears six times in the Quran, and every occurrence describes it descending rather than arising: onto the Prophet, onto believers at a moment of fear, or into a chest. The term is shared with related languages of the region, where a similar word names the divine presence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Help is presented as something that has already happened, which changes what the reluctant listener is being asked for. Their assistance is not needed for the outcome; it is offered to them as an opportunity. The ayah also locates support in things nobody saw, a calm and unseen forces, so the evidence for divine help is survival rather than spectacle. The two men are named only as a companion and a second.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for tranquillity sent down, after a moment when numbers had failed.
Describes the same descent of calm into believers' hearts, increasing their faith.
Shows a similar instruction not to grieve, given to the mother of Moses.

studies.applyIt: Think of a moment you got through that you had been certain you would not. You did not arrange the part that saved you. This ayah argues backwards from exactly that kind of memory, and keeping one specific instance in mind is more use in a crisis than any general statement about trust.

studies.title: Only What Is Written For Us
studies.meaning: The reply is short and its grammar does the work. Nothing reaches us except what God has written for us, with the preposition meaning for rather than against, so even hardship is placed on the side of what is given. Then a title, our guardian, and finally an instruction phrased in the third person rather than the second, which lets the sentence state a general rule instead of pressing a demand on the person hearing it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage about people who took satisfaction in setbacks falling on the community while keeping clear of anything costly themselves. This is the answer the Prophet is told to give them. The commentators read it as addressing an attitude rather than an event, and note that the reply concedes nothing about whether the setbacks were real.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something hitting its target, used of arrows and of rain. It presents events as arriving with an aim rather than as accidents, which is why the sentence can go on to name who sent them.

The preposition here means for rather than upon. Commentators note the choice: what is written is presented as assigned in a person's favour, which places even difficulty inside the category of what is given.
A word from the vocabulary of protection and clientage, used of the person responsible for someone with no other backing. It carries obligation rather than merely power, which is why it reassures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Clientage was a formal institution in Arabia. A person without a tribe attached themselves to a patron who guaranteed their safety and answered for their wrongs, and the relationship was public and binding. Naming God with that title was legally precise language rather than sentiment: it claimed a protector who could be called on and who had accepted the obligation.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction closing the ayah is phrased in the third person, telling believers what believers should do rather than addressing them directly. Arabic uses that form for stating a norm, and the Quran uses it sparingly. Here it lets a reply given to opponents double as a rule the community could take away from the exchange.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage neither denies hardship nor explains it. It relocates authorship, which is a different move: the question of why something happened is set aside for the question of whose it is. Naming God as guardian then adds obligation to power, so the claim is not merely that He controls events but that He has taken responsibility for the people inside them. Reliance follows as the reasonable response.

crossReferences.why: States that no misfortune occurs except as already recorded before it happens.
Adds that whoever believes has their heart guided through the misfortune.
Records the same reliance stated in the community's own words under threat.

studies.applyIt: Take the thing you are most afraid will happen and write one sentence describing it, then add the words that this too would be written for you rather than against you. You are not deciding it will not happen. You are testing whether the sentence changes anything, which is the only way to find out.

studies.title: Allies Of One Another
studies.meaning: The word used is not friendship but alliance, the term for people bound to protect and answer for one another. Men and women are named in the same clause and given the same standing in it. Five activities follow, and the first two are public: enjoining what is good and forbidding what is wrong, duties that belonged to people with standing rather than to dependants. The promise at the end carries a future marker, mercy still to come.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah. The ayah stands opposite an earlier description of the disaffected, who are said to be of one another in a matching construction, so the two groups are defined by the same grammar and distinguished by what they do together. The commentators point to that pairing, and read this ayah as the positive half of a deliberate contrast.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for the person who stands closest and takes responsibility, used of a guardian and of a patron. It names a relationship carrying obligations rather than an affection.
A verb of command rather than of suggestion. Giving it to the whole community, women included, distributes an authority that in that society belonged to heads of households and clan leaders.
The verb carries a prefix marking future time, which the commentators notice. Mercy is promised as coming rather than as already held, so the list preceding it is not presented as a receipt.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliance in Arabia was a formal act. Two parties or two clans swore mutual protection, and the bond obliged each to defend the other and to pay for their wrongs. It could be entered into by people with no blood relation, and in practice it outranked many family ties. Describing believing men and women as allies used the strongest available word for a bond that was chosen.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names believing men and believing women with separate words in a single clause, and the surah does the same for the disaffected a few ayat earlier. The pairing is not a stylistic habit; the Quran uses it where a claim about standing is being made, and the longest example runs ten such pairs in one ayah of surah 33.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Religious community is defined by mutual obligation rather than by shared belief alone, and the obligations named are public ones. Placing the duty to enjoin and forbid at the head of the list gives every member a share in the community's direction, which is a claim about who counts as responsible. The closing promise then keeps that from becoming self-congratulation by putting mercy in the future.

crossReferences.why: Describes the opposite group in a matching construction, defined by what they do together.
Extends the same pairing of men and women through ten qualities in one ayah.
Assigns the same public duty of calling to good to a group within the community.

studies.applyIt: Name one person in your community whose difficulty you know about and have been treating as their business rather than yours. Do one concrete thing about it this week, even a small one. The word this ayah uses is not friendship. It describes people who have accepted a claim on each other, and claims are met in specifics.

studies.title: He Takes The Charity Himself
studies.meaning: The question is rhetorical and slightly reproachful: do they not know. Two things are then stated as though they were obvious, and the second is the striking one. God accepts repentance, and God takes the charitable gifts, with a verb of receiving into the hand. The commentators note that the giving is described as passing to God rather than to the recipient, and that the ayah joins turning back and giving into one movement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah, in a passage about people who admitted their failure to join a difficult expedition and offered their wealth as amends. The ayah before instructs that a portion be taken from their property and that they be prayed for. This one answers the anxiety underneath: whether an offering made after a fault is received at all.

keyTerms.note: A verb for accepting something offered, used of a gift that is not refused. It implies a transaction that could have gone the other way, so acceptance is described as a decision rather than an automatic result.
The plain verb for taking in the hand. Using it of charitable gifts is as startling in Arabic as in English, since what is physically handed to a person is described as taken by God.
An intensive form of the same verb used of a human being turning back. God and the person are described with one root, so the turning is mutual, and His is the more frequent of the two.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Charity in Medina was physical and visible. Dates, grain and animals were brought and handed over in public, counted and distributed, and everyone knew who had given what. There was no anonymity in the transaction. Telling givers that the recipient of their sack of dates was God rather than the man holding out his hands reframed an exchange the whole town could watch.
studies.didYouKnow: The divine name closing this ayah comes from the same verb used for a person repenting, and the Quran uses that verb of God more often than of human beings. Arabic makes the reciprocity audible: the servant turns and the Lord turns, and the same three letters carry both movements in the same sentence.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Giving is described as received rather than merely observed, which changes its direction. The gift does not go down to someone in need with God watching; it goes to God, who then distributes it. That protects the dignity of the recipient and removes the giver's position of advantage in a single clause. Joining it to repentance makes a further point: material amends and inward turning are parts of one act.

crossReferences.why: Discusses giving openly and secretly, and what each does to a person's wrongs.
Precedes this ayah, instructing that a portion be taken from their wealth to purify them.
Repeats that He accepts repentance from His servants and pardons misdeeds.

studies.applyIt: Give something small this week to someone who will never know it came from you. A payment covered, a bill settled, something left where it is needed. The ayah says the transaction is not really between you and them, and giving anonymously is the simplest way to find out whether you believe that.

studies.title: A Purchase Already Agreed
studies.meaning: The relationship is described as a completed sale, with a buyer, a price and goods. What is bought is lives and property, and the payment is the Garden, stated as already settled rather than promised on condition. The terms are then said to stand in three scriptures, and a question is asked that has no available answer. The passage ends with an instruction to rejoice at the bargain, which the commentators read as its whole point.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, from a late surah addressing a community that had been asked to set out on a hard expedition and had divided over it. The commentators connect the language of a completed sale with the pledges given by early supporters in Medina before the migration, and note that the ayah addresses people who had already committed themselves rather than those being recruited.

keyTerms.note: A past-tense verb of purchase. The transaction is described as concluded rather than offered, which is why the closing instruction is to be glad about a sale already made rather than to consider one.
The word for a commercial exchange, and the root behind the pledge of allegiance, which was sealed by clasping hands the way traders did. Both senses are present in the sentence at once.
A phrase used across the Quran for final success. Its placement closes an ayah of commercial vocabulary with a word for winning through, which returns the exchange to the language of rescue.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca and Medina lived by trade, and a sale was a public ritual: terms stated aloud, hands struck together, witnesses present. A concluded sale could not be reopened, and a man who tried was disgraced. Describing commitment to God in that language spoke to people who knew exactly how binding a struck bargain was, and how little sympathy a seller with regrets received.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah names three scriptures together, the Torah, the Gospel and the Quran, and says the promise stands in all of them. It is one of the few places where the three are listed inside a single clause, and the sequence runs in chronological order, which presents the promise as long standing rather than new.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The transaction is described with God as the buyer, which is the strange part: the one who owns everything is portrayed as purchasing what is already His. Classical commentators read that as a statement about generosity rather than about exchange. And because the sale is announced as concluded, the passage is not recruiting anybody; it tells people what they are already inside, and asks them to be glad of it.

crossReferences.why: Offers the same image as a trade that saves from a painful punishment.
Uses the same commercial language of selling this life for the next.
Describes the pledge given by hand as a pledge given to God Himself.

studies.applyIt: Think of a commitment you made once and have been quietly renegotiating with yourself ever since. Do not reopen it today. Just notice that you have been treating a closed matter as an open one, and that most of the tiredness around it comes from holding the question open rather than from the commitment itself.

studies.title: Be With The Truthful
studies.meaning: Two instructions in a very short ayah, and the second is unusual. Not be truthful, but be with the truthful. The commentators note the difference: what is asked for is company, which places character in the plural. Some read the word as those who tell the truth, others as those whose whole state matches what they claim, and the Quran uses it in both senses. Nothing is said about how a person becomes such a one, only about proximity.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the account of three men who stayed behind from a difficult expedition and, unlike others, told the truth about why. The ayat just before describe their isolation and its end. The commentators read this instruction as the conclusion drawn from their case, which makes the truthful in question specific people the audience could name.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth and for what is solid and reliable. The word covers honest speech and a life that matches it, and the same root gives the term used for a formal charitable gift.
A plain preposition of company. Its use makes the instruction relational: the reader is not told to become something but to be near people who already are, and the difference is clearly deliberate.
From a root for shielding oneself. It is paired here with the command about company, so an inward disposition and an outward association are placed side by side as a single instruction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation in a town the size of Medina was cumulative and unforgettable. Everyone knew who had spoken accurately about a bad harvest and who had shaded it, and a man's word decided whether he could borrow, marry well, or lead. The three men who admitted staying behind took the harder route in a place where their admission would be remembered by everyone for years.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the last ayah of the long passage about the expedition and the people who did not join it, a passage running for dozens of ayat. The surah then turns to a short description of the messenger and ends. The instruction here is among the shortest sentences in the surah, and it arrives at the hinge between the two parts.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is presented as something maintained by company rather than by resolve alone. That is a claim about how people actually change: not by deciding to be truthful but by spending time where truthfulness is ordinary. It also makes the instruction available to someone who is not yet what they should be, since being near a quality comes before possessing it. Awareness of God is placed first, and the two are given together.

crossReferences.why: Names the truthful among the company promised to those who obey.
Precedes it, describing the three whose truthfulness this instruction follows from.
Describes men true to what they pledged, and God rewarding the truthful for their truth.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your unstructured time goes and identify one person or group that makes exaggeration feel normal, and one that makes it feel awkward. Spend an extra hour this week with the second. The ayah does not ask you to be better on your own; it points at the room you are standing in.

studies.title: A Messenger From Among You
studies.meaning: Four descriptions in a single line, and the first is about origin: he is from among yourselves, which the commentators read as one of you rather than a stranger sent in. Then his hardship at your hardship, using a word for something weighing heavily. Then eagerness for you. The last two terms are divine names elsewhere in the Quran, applied here to a human being, which is rare and which the commentators remark on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, the second to last ayah of the surah and, according to several reports, among the final passages of the Quran to be revealed. The surah has been severe throughout, dealing with people who withheld and evaded, and it closes by turning to the character of the man who had been doing the asking. The commentators note the contrast between the surah's tone and its ending.

keyTerms.note: The phrase means something is hard for him to bear. The same word elsewhere describes might and rarity, so the sentence says your difficulty is costly to him, in the vocabulary of value.
A strong word, used elsewhere of greed and of clinging to life. Applied to his concern for people, it describes an appetite rather than a duty, which is what makes the description warm.
A word for gentleness towards someone in difficulty, finer than the general term for mercy. It is used of God in many places, and here it is given to a man, paired with the word for mercy.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A leader in Arabia was expected to be formidable, generous and unmoved. Poetry praised chiefs for endurance and for hospitality, not for anxiety about their followers' distress. Grief expressed on someone else's behalf belonged to the public rituals of mourning. Describing a leader as troubled by what troubles his people named something the surrounding culture did not obviously admire.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words closing this ayah are both used of God elsewhere in the Quran, and this is one of very few places where such a pair is applied to a human being. Classical commentators note the point, treating the shared vocabulary as a statement about the messenger's role rather than about his nature.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophecy is described here through temperament rather than through miracle or authority. What qualifies the messenger, in this sentence, is that other people's suffering costs him something. Naming his origin first makes the same point structurally: the message is not delivered from outside the human situation but from inside it. And placing this at the end of a severe surah suggests the severity was never separable from the concern.

crossReferences.why: Explains the same gentleness as a mercy from God and shows what it prevented.
States his sending as a mercy to all the worlds, in a single line.
Describes him almost destroying himself out of concern that they will not believe.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose difficulty you know about and have filed under sympathy rather than cost. Let it be expensive for an hour: sit with what it would actually be like. The ayah describes a man for whom other people's hardship was heavy, and it names that weight as the qualification, not as a side effect.
